title: General Security Concepts
intro:
Domain 1 is the vocabulary and mental model for everything else on the SY0-701 exam. It covers how we classify security controls, the fundamental goals of security (confidentiality, integrity, availability, non-repudiation), how identity and access are managed, why organisations do gap analyses and adopt Zero Trust, how physical security and deception technologies fit in, why change management exists, and how cryptography actually protects data. At 12 percent of the exam it is the smallest domain by weight, but its concepts are reused constantly in Domains 2 through 5, so a weak foundation here costs you points everywhere.

The exam tests this domain mostly through scenario questions: you are given a short story about an organisation and asked to identify which control type, which security property, or which cryptographic tool is being described. The trap is that many of the terms sound alike. A preventive control and a deterrent control both aim to stop bad things, but they work differently. Hashing and encryption both scramble data, but only one is reversible. Symmetric and asymmetric encryption both protect confidentiality, but they solve different key-management problems. Learning to draw those distinctions crisply is the whole game in Domain 1.

Study approach: watch each Professor Messer video, then read the matching deep dive here and work through the three quiz questions. Write your own one-line definition of every key term without looking. For a future SOC analyst or GRC analyst in a Nigerian bank or fintech, this domain also maps directly onto real work: control classification is the language of audits and CBN or ISO 27001 compliance, AAA and Zero Trust are what your identity and network teams argue about daily, and PKI and hashing are what you will be reading in logs and certificate alerts.

objectives.title: Compare and contrast various types of security controls

videos.title: Security Controls
videos.summary: Messer introduces the four control categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and the six control types (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive), with a grid of examples showing how any single control can be described by both a category and a type.
videos.deepDive:
A security control is anything an organisation puts in place to reduce risk: a firewall, a policy document, a locked door, a security guard, a training programme. Because there are thousands of possible controls, the industry classifies them along two independent axes so we can talk about coverage and gaps precisely. The first axis is the category, which answers 'who or what implements this control?'. The second axis is the type, which answers 'what does this control do to an attack?'. Every control has exactly one category and at least one type, and the exam loves to ask you to identify both from a scenario.

The four categories. Technical controls are implemented by systems: firewalls, antivirus, encryption, access control lists, intrusion prevention. Managerial controls are the administrative side: security policies, risk assessments, standard operating procedures, the decision to require background checks. Operational controls are carried out by people rather than systems: security guards, awareness training, change-management meetings, log review by an analyst. Physical controls limit physical access: fences, bollards, badge readers, access control vestibules, locks. A quick test: if you removed all the people, would the control still work? If yes, it is technical or physical. If it is a written rule or plan, it is managerial. If a human has to do something for it to work, it is operational.

The six types. A preventive control stops the event from happening at all (a firewall rule that blocks port 23, a locked door, a policy that forbids USB drives). A deterrent control discourages the attacker but does not physically stop them (a warning banner, a 'this area is monitored' sign, a visible camera housing). A detective control identifies that something has happened or is happening (IDS alerts, log review, motion sensors, an internal audit). A corrective control fixes or limits the damage after the fact (restoring from backup, patching after an incident, a fire extinguisher). A compensating control is an alternative used when the primary control is not feasible; for example, an old core banking module that cannot be patched is isolated behind a strict firewall and monitored closely. A directive control tells people what to do: a policy, a sign reading 'authorised personnel only', mandatory training.

Worked example. A Lagos fintech installs a badge reader on the server-room door (physical, preventive), hangs a sign saying the room is under CCTV (physical, deterrent), reviews the door logs every morning (operational, detective), keeps an offsite backup to rebuild servers (technical, corrective), publishes a clean-desk policy (managerial, directive), and, because a legacy switch cannot support 802.1X, places it in its own VLAN with extra logging (technical, compensating). Notice how the same category appears with different types and vice versa. Also notice that a control can serve more than one type: a visible camera both deters and detects.

Common confusions. Preventive versus deterrent: prevention works even if the attacker does not care; deterrence only works if the attacker notices and decides not to try. Detective versus corrective: detection tells you it happened; correction restores you afterward. Directive versus managerial: directive is a type (it instructs behaviour), managerial is a category (it is administrative in nature). Most directive controls are also managerial, but a physical sign is a physical directive control. For GRC work, this grid is what you use to map an organisation's controls against a framework such as ISO 27001 Annex A or the CBN risk-based cybersecurity framework and spot where a whole type (often detective or corrective) is missing.

keyTerms.def: A control implemented and enforced by systems or software, such as a firewall, encryption, or an access control list.
An administrative control that governs security through policy, planning, and risk decisions, such as a security policy or risk assessment.
A control carried out primarily by people in day-to-day operations, such as security guards, awareness training, or manual log review.
A control that restricts physical access to facilities or equipment, such as fences, locks, bollards, and badge readers.
A control that stops an unwanted event from occurring in the first place.
A control that discourages an attacker from attempting an action without physically preventing it.
A control that identifies and records that a security event has occurred or is occurring.
A control that restores systems or limits damage after a security event has occurred.
An alternative control that provides equivalent protection when the primary or required control cannot be implemented.
A control that directs or mandates behaviour, typically through policies, procedures, or signage.

examTips: Expect a scenario and be asked for BOTH the category and the type; read for who implements it (category) and what it does to the attack timeline (type).
Deterrent controls only work if the attacker sees them; if the control would stop a blind attacker, it is preventive.
A compensating control is always a substitute for something that could not be done; look for words like 'cannot be patched' or 'legacy system'.
Backups and restore procedures are the classic corrective control; audits, logs, and IDS are the classic detective controls.
One control can hold multiple types (a camera is deterrent and detective); pick the type that the question stem emphasises.
videos.realWorld: In a bank's GRC team, the control grid is the daily language of audits. When an auditor asks 'what controls do you have over privileged access?', the expected answer covers a managerial policy, a technical PAM tool that enforces it, an operational quarterly access review by people, and detective logging into the SIEM. A SOC analyst lives mostly in detective controls (SIEM alerts, EDR telemetry) and triggers corrective ones (isolate a host, restore a file share), so knowing the vocabulary helps you write incident reports that GRC and management understand.

quiz.q: A fintech in Lagos discovers that a payment-gateway server runs an application that cannot be upgraded for another year. To reduce risk, the security team places the server in an isolated network segment with a strict firewall and enables enhanced logging. Which type of control best describes this action?
quiz.explain: The required control (patching the application) cannot be applied, so the team substitutes an alternative that provides similar risk reduction. That is the definition of a compensating control. It is not corrective because nothing has gone wrong yet, not deterrent because attackers are not being discouraged by visibility, and not directive because no behaviour is being mandated.

quiz.q: A company posts a sign at its data-centre entrance stating that all activity is recorded and violators will be prosecuted. No camera is actually installed. Which category and type of control is this?
quiz.explain: The sign is a physical object placed to discourage attackers, so it is a physical deterrent. It cannot prevent entry, and with no camera it cannot detect anything. It is not managerial because it is not a policy or administrative decision, and while a sign can be directive, the emphasis of the scenario is on discouraging violators.

quiz.q: After a ransomware incident, an IT team restores encrypted file servers from the previous night's backup. Which control type does the restoration represent?
quiz.explain: Restoring from backup limits the damage after the event has already occurred, which is the purpose of a corrective control. Preventive controls would have stopped the ransomware, detective controls would have identified it, and compensating controls substitute for a control that could not be implemented.

videos.title: The CIA Triad
videos.summary: Messer explains the three core goals of information security, confidentiality, integrity, and availability, and gives examples of the technologies that support each one.
videos.deepDive:
The CIA triad is the oldest and most durable way of describing what security is trying to achieve. Every control, every incident, and every risk can be described in terms of which of these three properties it protects or threatens. If you cannot say which leg of the triad a control supports, you probably do not understand the control yet.

Confidentiality means that information is only readable by those who are authorised. The threats are disclosure, snooping, and theft of data. The tools are encryption (data at rest and in transit), access controls (permissions, ACLs, need-to-know), and two-factor authentication to make sure the person reading the data is who they claim to be. A leaked customer database is a confidentiality failure. Note that confidentiality is not the same as privacy: privacy is the individual's right to control their data, confidentiality is the organisation's ability to keep it from unauthorised eyes; the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) requires the second in order to deliver the first.

Integrity means that data has not been altered by anyone unauthorised, and that if it is altered you can tell. The threats are tampering, corruption, and unauthorised modification. The tools are hashing (a fingerprint that changes if a single bit changes), digital signatures (a hash protected by a private key so it also proves who produced it), certificates, and non-repudiation. A worked example: a bank sends a wire-transfer instruction to a correspondent bank. If an attacker changes the account number in transit, that is an integrity attack. A digital signature over the message would make the change detectable, because the hash would no longer match. Integrity also includes data being complete and consistent, which is why database constraints and transaction logs are integrity controls as well.

Availability means that systems and data are there when authorised users need them. The threats are denial of service, hardware failure, ransomware (which attacks availability by making data unreadable), and even power cuts. The tools are redundancy, fault tolerance, patching (so systems do not crash or get exploited), backups, load balancing, and generators. A payment switch that goes down at month-end salary time is an availability failure that customers notice immediately.

Why the triad matters for decisions. The three properties often pull against each other. Strong encryption improves confidentiality but adds latency and key-management complexity that can hurt availability. Aggressive patching improves availability long-term but a bad patch can break a system today. Requiring approvals for every change improves integrity but slows the business. Security work is largely about choosing the balance for a given asset, and that is why classification and risk assessment come first. Some frameworks extend the triad with non-repudiation, authenticity, and accountability (sometimes called the CIA-NA or the hexad), but the exam still centres on the three.

Contrast to memorise. Encryption protects confidentiality; hashing protects integrity; redundancy protects availability. If a question describes a control and asks what it protects, map it to the tool list above. If a question describes an attack, ask what the attacker gained: reading (confidentiality), changing (integrity), or blocking (availability).

keyTerms.def: The property that information is disclosed only to authorised individuals, systems, or processes.
The property that data is accurate, complete, and has not been modified without authorisation, and that any modification is detectable.
The property that systems, services, and data are accessible to authorised users when required.
Transforming data with a key so it is unreadable without the corresponding key; the primary control for confidentiality.
Producing a fixed-length fingerprint of data so any change can be detected; the primary control for integrity.
Duplicating components or systems so that a single failure does not interrupt service; a primary control for availability.
Restricting who can read, write, or execute a resource, supporting both confidentiality and integrity.
The ability of a system to keep operating correctly when one or more of its components fail.

examTips: Map tools to properties: encryption = confidentiality, hashing and signatures = integrity, redundancy and backups = availability.
Ransomware is usually tested as an availability attack (data is unreadable) even though it involves encryption.
Look for the verb in the scenario: read or leak (C), change or alter (I), outage or delay (A).
Do not confuse confidentiality with privacy; the exam treats privacy as a separate legal and governance concept.
When a scenario mentions a business decision that trades one property for another, the correct answer usually involves risk assessment or classification.
videos.realWorld: SOC analysts triage alerts by triad impact: a data exfiltration alert is a confidentiality event and drives a breach-notification clock under NDPA, a tampered configuration file is an integrity event and drives forensics, and a DDoS against the internet banking portal is an availability event and drives capacity and upstream scrubbing. GRC teams use the same lens when classifying assets, because a payment ledger has extreme integrity requirements while a marketing website mostly needs availability.

quiz.q: A bank discovers that an insider modified the beneficiary account numbers in a batch of outgoing transfers before they were processed. Which security property was primarily violated?
quiz.explain: The data was altered without authorisation, which is an integrity violation. Confidentiality would involve unauthorised disclosure, availability would involve the transfers being blocked or delayed, and non-repudiation concerns proving who performed an action, which is related but not the primary property broken here.

quiz.q: A fintech wants to ensure that its mobile app can still process payments even if one of its data-centre nodes fails. Which control most directly supports the security property at stake?
options: Redundant servers behind a load balancer
quiz.explain: The requirement is that service continues despite a failure, which is availability. Redundancy behind a load balancer directly supports availability. Encryption supports confidentiality, hashing supports integrity, and MFA supports authentication and confidentiality.

quiz.q: Customer records on a laptop were exposed when the laptop was stolen from a car. Which control would have best protected the property that was violated?
quiz.explain: The violated property is confidentiality, because unauthorised people could read the records. Full-disk encryption keeps the data unreadable without the key. Backups and a hot site address availability, and file integrity monitoring addresses integrity.

videos.title: Non-repudiation
videos.summary: Messer explains how proof of integrity (hashing) and proof of origin (digital signatures) combine to give non-repudiation, so a sender cannot later deny having sent a message.
videos.deepDive:
To repudiate something is to deny it. Non-repudiation is the security property that prevents a party from plausibly denying that they performed an action, sent a message, or agreed to a transaction. In banking this is not an abstract idea: when a customer says 'I never authorised that transfer', the bank needs evidence strong enough to hold up to a regulator or a court. Non-repudiation is the technical basis for that evidence.

Two building blocks. Non-repudiation requires two things at once. First, proof of integrity: the message that exists now is exactly the message that was sent. Hashing gives us this. If you hash a document and later re-hash it and the values match, the document is unchanged. But a hash on its own proves nothing about who created it, because anyone can compute a hash. Second, proof of origin: the message really came from the claimed sender. This is what a digital signature provides. The sender hashes the message and then encrypts that hash with their private key. Anyone with the sender's public key can decrypt the signature, recover the hash, and compare it with their own hash of the message. If they match, two things are proven at once: the message is unchanged (integrity) and only the holder of the private key could have produced that signature (origin and authenticity). Because the private key is never shared, the sender cannot credibly claim someone else signed it.

Why symmetric keys cannot give non-repudiation. This is the contrast the exam likes. A message authentication code (HMAC) uses a shared secret key. It proves integrity and proves that someone holding the shared key created the message. But both parties hold that key, so either of them could have created it. The receiver cannot prove to a third party that the sender, and not the receiver, produced the message. Only asymmetric signatures, where the signing key belongs to exactly one party, achieve non-repudiation.

Worked example. A corporate customer submits a bulk payroll file through a bank's portal. The file is hashed with SHA-256 and the customer's browser signs the hash with a private key stored on a smart card or in a hardware token. The bank verifies the signature using the customer's certificate. Months later the customer disputes the payroll. The bank produces the file, the signature, the certificate chain, and the timestamp. The customer cannot reasonably deny it, because only their private key could have produced that signature. Add a trusted timestamp and audit logs and you have a full non-repudiation package.

Limits and caveats. Non-repudiation assumes the private key was under the sole control of its owner. If the key was stolen, or stored on a shared machine, the argument weakens. That is why key protection, certificate revocation, and hardware tokens matter. It also depends on trusted logs and clocks, so log integrity and NTP are part of the real-world non-repudiation story. Finally, note the vocabulary: authenticity says the message came from the claimed source; non-repudiation goes one step further and says the source cannot deny it. Digital signatures deliver both.

keyTerms.def: Assurance that a party cannot deny having performed an action or sent a message, typically achieved with digital signatures.
Evidence, usually a hash, that data has not been changed since it was created or sent.
Evidence that a message genuinely came from the claimed sender, provided by a digital signature.
A hash of a message encrypted with the sender's private key, verifiable with the sender's public key.
The secret half of an asymmetric key pair, used to sign and to decrypt; never shared.
The shareable half of an asymmetric key pair, used to verify signatures and to encrypt.
A hash-based message authentication code using a shared secret key; proves integrity and authenticity but not non-repudiation.
Assurance that data or a message originates from the claimed source.

examTips: Non-repudiation always points to digital signatures and therefore to asymmetric cryptography and the sender's private key.
Hashing alone gives integrity but not non-repudiation; HMAC gives integrity and authenticity but not non-repudiation because the key is shared.
The signature is created with the private key and verified with the public key; reverse that and you have encryption for confidentiality.
If a question asks how to prove a specific user sent an email, the answer is a digital signature (S/MIME), not encryption.
videos.realWorld: Fraud investigations in banks lean on non-repudiation evidence: signed transaction requests, OTP logs tied to a registered device, and immutable audit trails in the core banking system. A SOC analyst may be asked to pull those artefacts during a dispute, and a GRC analyst will check that the logs are retained, time-synchronised, and protected from alteration so they remain defensible under the CBN and NDPA rules on record keeping.

quiz.q: A CFO claims she never approved a vendor payment that was submitted through the finance portal. Which control would most directly allow the bank to prove she did?
options: The payment record was hashed with SHA-256
The payment record was encrypted with AES-256
The payment request was digitally signed with the CFO's private key
The payment was authenticated with an HMAC shared between the CFO and the bank
quiz.explain: A digital signature made with the CFO's private key can only have been produced by the holder of that key, which gives non-repudiation. A hash alone proves integrity, not origin. Encryption provides confidentiality. An HMAC uses a key shared with the bank, so the bank itself could have produced it and the CFO could repudiate.

quiz.q: Two systems exchange messages protected with an HMAC using a shared secret. Which security property is NOT provided by this arrangement?
quiz.explain: HMAC provides integrity and authenticity (the message came from someone holding the key and was not changed). Because both parties hold the same key, either could have generated the MAC, so neither can prove to a third party which one sent it. Non-repudiation requires a key held by only one party.

quiz.q: A user receives a digitally signed document. What does the user use to verify the signature?
quiz.explain: Signatures are created with the sender's private key and verified with the sender's public key. The sender's private key is never distributed, the recipient's private key is only used to decrypt messages sent to the recipient, and symmetric keys are not used for digital signatures.

videos.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting
videos.summary: Messer walks through the AAA framework: proving who you are (authentication), deciding what you may do (authorization), and logging what you did (accounting), including how devices authenticate using certificates and how authorization models scale.
videos.deepDive:
AAA is the framework behind almost every login you have ever performed, and the exam expects you to keep the three A's separate even though they happen within seconds of each other. The trick is to remember the question each one answers. Identification answers 'who do you claim to be?' (a username). Authentication answers 'prove it' (a password, a fingerprint, an OTP). Authorization answers 'now that we know who you are, what are you allowed to do?' (read this folder, approve transfers up to a limit). Accounting answers 'what did you actually do, and when?' (logs of logins, resources accessed, data transferred).

Authentication. The common architecture is a client, a network access device (VPN concentrator, wireless controller, switch), and a central authentication server such as RADIUS, TACACS+, or an LDAP directory like Active Directory. The client presents credentials, the access device forwards them, and the server checks them against its database. Centralising authentication means one place to disable a leaver and one set of logs to review. Authentication factors are something you know, have, are, and the attributes somewhere you are and something you do; combining two or more different factors is multifactor authentication.

Authenticating systems, not just people. A recurring exam topic is how a device proves its identity when there is no human to type a password. The answer is a digitally signed certificate. The organisation runs its own certificate authority (CA), issues a certificate to each managed laptop or server, and the device presents that certificate when it connects. Because the certificate is signed by the CA's private key, the access device can verify it against the CA's public key. Anything without a valid certificate is not on the trusted list. This is the basis of 802.1X network access control and of many VPN and MDM deployments.

Authorization models. Assigning permissions to each user individually does not scale and produces errors. Instead, users are placed into groups or roles, and permissions are attached to the role. A new teller gets the Teller role and inherits exactly what tellers need; when she is promoted, her role changes. This abstraction between the user and the resource is what makes least privilege manageable, and the exam expects you to know that role-based access is the scalable solution. Authorization can also be conditional: same user, but a different level of access from an unmanaged device or an unusual location.

Accounting. Accounting is the audit trail: who logged in, from where, for how long, what they accessed, how much data they moved. It supports non-repudiation, incident investigation, billing, and compliance evidence. Without accounting you cannot prove that authorization actually worked. In practice, accounting records flow to a SIEM, where the SOC correlates them with other telemetry.

Contrast to lock in. Authentication failing means 'we do not believe you are who you say'. Authorization failing means 'we believe you, but you may not do that'. A 401 error is authentication, a 403 is authorization. A scenario where a valid user opens a file she should not see is an authorization problem, not an authentication one, and the fix is permissions or roles rather than stronger passwords.

keyTerms.def: Claiming an identity, typically by presenting a username or account name.
Proving a claimed identity using one or more factors such as a password, token, or biometric.
Determining what an authenticated identity is permitted to access or do.
Recording user and system activity such as logins, resource access, and session duration for audit and analysis.
A category of evidence used to authenticate: something you know, have, or are, plus attributes like location or behaviour.
Authentication requiring evidence from two or more different factor categories.
Granting permissions to roles or groups rather than to individuals so that access scales and follows job function.
A common centralised authentication, authorization, and accounting protocol used by network access devices.
A CA-signed certificate installed on a device so the device itself can be authenticated without human credentials.

examTips: Separate the questions: who are you (identification), prove it (authentication), what may you do (authorization), what did you do (accounting).
Two passwords are still one factor; MFA needs different factor categories.
When a scenario asks how devices without users prove identity, the answer is a certificate issued by an internal CA.
Scaling permissions across many users points to roles or groups, not per-user ACL entries.
Accounting is the source of audit logs; if the question wants evidence of what happened, that is accounting.
videos.realWorld: A SOC analyst spends much of the day reading AAA data: RADIUS and VPN logs, Active Directory authentication events (4624, 4625, 4768), and privileged session recordings. Spotting a successful login after many failures, or a teller role suddenly accessing a treasury system, depends on understanding which A each log line represents. GRC analysts audit authorization by running quarterly user-access reviews against role definitions, which regulators such as the CBN expect banks to evidence.

quiz.q: An employee logs into the HR system successfully but receives an error when trying to open the executive payroll report. Which AAA element is responsible for this outcome?
quiz.explain: The user was successfully authenticated (the login worked), so the block on the payroll report is a permissions decision, which is authorization. Identification is the username claim, and accounting is the logging of the attempt.

quiz.q: A company wants to ensure that only corporate-owned laptops can connect to its VPN, even if a valid username and password are supplied. What should the company deploy?
options: Accounting logs sent to a SIEM
Digitally signed device certificates issued by an internal CA
A shared pre-shared key for the VPN
quiz.explain: Device authentication is done with a certificate issued by the organisation's CA and installed on each managed laptop; the VPN verifies the signature. Passwords authenticate the user, not the device. A pre-shared key could be copied to any machine, and accounting logs record activity rather than restrict access.

quiz.q: A bank has 4,000 employees and finds that permissions assigned individually are frequently wrong and slow to update. Which approach best addresses this?
options: Require multifactor authentication for all users
Store all user permissions in a spreadsheet for review
Increase the frequency of accounting log reviews
Assign permissions to roles and place users into the appropriate roles
quiz.explain: Role-based authorization scales because permissions are attached to a role that reflects a job function; a user is simply added to or removed from the role. MFA strengthens authentication, not authorization. A spreadsheet does not enforce anything, and log reviews detect problems rather than prevent them.

videos.title: Gap Analysis
videos.summary: Messer describes a gap analysis as a structured comparison between where an organisation's security currently is and where it needs to be, driven by a chosen baseline or framework, and ending in a prioritised report.
videos.deepDive:
A gap analysis is the formal process of answering three questions: where are we now, where do we need to be, and what is the difference? In security the 'where we need to be' is usually defined by a framework or standard (ISO 27001, NIST Cybersecurity Framework, PCI DSS for card data, the CBN risk-based cybersecurity framework for Nigerian banks, or an internal baseline). The output is a list of gaps ranked by risk, with a plan and cost for closing each one. It is fundamentally a GRC activity, but SOC teams are frequently the people who supply the evidence.

Step one: choose the baseline. A gap analysis without a target is just a wish list. The baseline might be external (a regulator or a customer contract demands PCI DSS compliance before you can process cards) or internal (management decides every server must meet a hardening standard). The baseline determines what counts as a gap. This is why the first exam-relevant fact about gap analysis is that it starts with a defined goal or framework.

Step two: gather the current state. This is the slow part. It involves interviewing people, reviewing policies, examining system configurations, running vulnerability scans, and reading logs. People are as important as technology: a control that exists on paper but that nobody follows is a gap. A thorough analysis also looks at the training and experience of the team, because a SIEM with no one able to tune it is not really a detective control. Breaking the organisation into logical units (departments, business lines, systems) keeps this manageable.

Step three: compare and evaluate. For each requirement in the baseline, record whether the organisation fully meets it, partially meets it, or does not meet it, and note the evidence. Weaknesses are then scored by how much risk they carry so that the most damaging gaps come first rather than the easiest ones. A missing privileged-access review is more urgent than a missing screensaver policy.

Step four: the report. The final deliverable is a document that states the current state, the desired state, each gap, the recommended remediation, the cost, the owner, and a timeline. Executives read the summary and roadmap; engineers read the detail. This document becomes the input to budgeting and to the risk register, and it is re-run periodically to show progress.

Worked example. A Nigerian fintech applying for a Payment Service Provider licence is told it must align with ISO 27001. A consultant maps the 93 Annex A controls against the company. Findings include: no formal asset inventory (gap, high), MFA only on email but not on the admin console (partial, high), no tested backup restore (gap, high), and an acceptable-use policy that exists but was never signed by staff (partial, medium). The report proposes closing the high gaps within 90 days and gives an estimated cost. Six months later the analysis is repeated to evidence closure.

Do not confuse. A gap analysis is broader than a vulnerability scan (which finds technical flaws in systems) and different from a penetration test (which simulates an attacker). It is also not a risk assessment, although the two feed each other: the gap analysis finds missing controls, the risk assessment weighs what those gaps could cost. On the exam, if the question describes comparing a current environment against a chosen standard and producing a report, the answer is gap analysis.

keyTerms.def: A structured comparison of an organisation's current security posture against a desired state defined by a framework or baseline, producing a prioritised list of shortfalls.
The defined set of requirements or minimum configuration that an organisation measures itself against.
A published structure of security controls or practices, such as NIST CSF or ISO 27001, used as the target for a gap analysis.
The documented condition of people, processes, and technology as they exist today.
The target condition the organisation must reach to meet its chosen baseline or framework.
The prioritised list of actions, owners, costs, and timelines to close identified gaps.
A living document listing identified risks, their ratings, owners, and treatment decisions; gap analysis findings feed it.

examTips: A gap analysis always begins by choosing the standard or baseline to compare against; without that there is no gap to measure.
It evaluates people and processes, not just technology; an unfollowed policy is a gap.
The end product is a formal report with a prioritised roadmap, not a list of patched systems.
Distinguish it from a vulnerability scan (technical flaws) and a penetration test (simulated attack).
videos.realWorld: GRC analysts in banks run gap analyses constantly: against the CBN cybersecurity framework, ISO 27001 before certification, PCI DSS before a card-scheme audit, and NDPA for data protection. The analyst builds a control-by-control spreadsheet, requests evidence from IT and the SOC (screenshots, configs, log samples), rates each control, and drafts the roadmap. SOC analysts feel the other end: a gap finding that says 'no alerting on privileged account creation' becomes a new SIEM detection rule they must build and evidence.

quiz.q: A fintech is preparing for ISO 27001 certification and hires a consultant to determine which of the standard's controls it does not currently meet. What is the consultant performing?
quiz.explain: Comparing the current environment against a defined standard to identify missing or partial controls is a gap analysis. A penetration test simulates attacks, a vulnerability scan finds technical weaknesses on systems, and a business impact analysis measures the effect of disruption on business processes.

quiz.q: During a gap analysis, an auditor finds that a bank has a well-written acceptable-use policy but that no employee has ever read or signed it. How should this be recorded?
options: As fully compliant, because the policy exists
As a gap, because the control is not operating
As not applicable, because policies are managerial
As a vulnerability to be patched
quiz.explain: A gap analysis assesses whether controls actually work, including the people and process elements. A policy nobody follows is not an effective control, so it is a gap (or at best partial). The existence of a document does not make it compliant, and the term vulnerability refers to technical weaknesses.

quiz.q: Which of the following must be established FIRST before a security gap analysis can be conducted?
options: The baseline or framework to compare against
quiz.explain: The desired state, defined by a baseline or framework, is the reference against which gaps are measured, so it must be chosen first. Costs and the report come at the end, and penetration test results are an optional input rather than a prerequisite.

videos.title: Zero Trust
videos.summary: Messer introduces the Zero Trust model, where nothing inside the network is trusted by default, and explains the planes of operation, adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control, and the policy engine, policy administrator, and policy enforcement point.
videos.deepDive:
Traditional network security worked like a castle: a hard perimeter firewall and a soft, trusted interior. Once an attacker (or a phished employee's laptop) was inside, they could move laterally almost freely. Zero Trust is the response. Its core rule is that no user, device, or connection is trusted because of where it sits on the network. Every request for access is authenticated, authorised, and encrypted, every time, regardless of whether it comes from the internet or from the desk next to the server room. The model is described in NIST SP 800-207, and the SY0-701 exam uses its vocabulary.

Two planes. Zero Trust architectures separate the data plane from the control plane. The data plane is where the actual traffic flows and where devices such as switches, routers, and firewalls forward packets. The control plane is where the decisions are made about what is allowed: the policies, the identity checks, the rules. Separating them means that a decision about whether a user may reach a database is made centrally by the control plane and then enforced at many points in the data plane.

Control plane components. The policy engine is the brain: it evaluates every access request against policy and against signals such as identity, device health, and threat intelligence, and returns grant, deny, or revoke. The policy administrator takes that decision and communicates it to the enforcement side, for example by issuing a session token or telling the gateway to open the path. Together they are sometimes called the policy decision point. In the data plane, the policy enforcement point (PEP) is the gatekeeper that actually allows or blocks the traffic, such as a gateway, an agent on the device, or a firewall. The subject (user or application) sends a request through the PEP; the PEP asks the policy decision point; the decision comes back; the PEP enforces it.

Adaptive identity. Instead of a simple pass or fail on a password, the policy engine considers context: is this the user's usual device, is the location plausible, is the time of day normal, what is the sensitivity of the resource? A login from an unknown device in another country to the core banking admin console might trigger step-up authentication or be denied outright, while the same user opening the intranet from their managed laptop in the office is allowed silently.

Threat scope reduction and implicit trust zones. Zero Trust limits how far a compromise can spread by giving each identity access only to the specific resources it needs, which is least privilege applied at network scale. Networks are broken into small segments, and connections cross zone boundaries only after a policy check. An implicit trust zone is the small area where traffic is allowed to flow without re-authentication, such as between a PEP and the resource it protects; the aim is to keep those zones as small as possible.

Policy-driven access control. All of this is expressed as policy rather than as static firewall rules tied to IP addresses. Policies reference users, groups, device posture, and application identity, which is why they survive cloud migrations and remote work. Do not confuse Zero Trust with a single product: it is an architecture that uses MFA, micro-segmentation, identity providers, EDR, and encryption together. For a bank with staff working from home and services in the cloud, it is the model that replaces the broken castle.

keyTerms.def: A security model in which no user, device, or connection is trusted by default and every access request is verified regardless of network location.
The part of a Zero Trust architecture that defines policy and makes access decisions.
The part of the architecture where traffic actually flows and where access decisions are enforced.
The control-plane component that evaluates each access request against policy and signals and decides grant, deny, or revoke.
The control-plane component that communicates the policy engine's decision to the enforcement point, for example by issuing session credentials.
The data-plane gatekeeper that allows or blocks a subject's connection based on the decision received from the control plane.
Authentication and authorisation that adjust based on context such as device, location, behaviour, and resource sensitivity.
Limiting the blast radius of a compromise by granting minimal access and segmenting the environment.
A small region within which traffic is allowed to flow without additional policy checks, typically between an enforcement point and the resource it protects.

examTips: Decisions happen in the control plane (policy engine plus policy administrator); enforcement happens in the data plane (policy enforcement point).
If the question mentions considering location, device, or behaviour before granting access, the answer is adaptive identity.
Segmenting the network to limit lateral movement is threat scope reduction.
Zero Trust is a model, not a product; answers naming a single firewall are usually wrong.
The exam borrows terms from NIST SP 800-207; the policy decision point is the engine and administrator together.
videos.realWorld: Many Nigerian banks and fintechs are mid-way through Zero Trust programmes: identity providers with conditional access, EDR posture checks before VPN or SaaS access, and micro-segmentation around the core banking and payment switch environments. A SOC analyst sees the policy engine's decisions as deny and step-up events in the identity logs and investigates unusual ones. A GRC analyst maps the programme to the CBN framework's access-control and network-segmentation requirements and tracks which zones still rely on implicit trust.

quiz.q: In a Zero Trust architecture, a user's request to reach a payroll application is evaluated against policy, device health, and the user's normal behaviour before a decision is returned. Which component performs this evaluation?
quiz.explain: The policy engine in the control plane evaluates the request against policy and contextual signals and produces the grant or deny decision. The policy enforcement point only enforces that decision, data-plane devices move traffic, and an implicit trust zone is a region where checks are not repeated.

quiz.q: A bank wants a login from an employee's usual laptop in the office to proceed silently, while the same login from an unrecognised device abroad triggers additional authentication. Which Zero Trust concept does this describe?
quiz.explain: Adjusting authentication and access requirements based on context such as device, location, and behaviour is adaptive identity. Threat scope reduction concerns limiting lateral movement, the policy administrator communicates decisions, and control plane separation is an architectural principle rather than the contextual behaviour described.

quiz.q: Which of the following BEST describes the role of a policy enforcement point in a Zero Trust design?
options: It issues session tokens after a decision is made
It allows or blocks the subject's traffic based on the decision from the control plane
It stores threat-intelligence feeds used in decisions
It defines the organisation's access policies
quiz.explain: The policy enforcement point sits in the data plane and acts on the decision it receives, permitting or denying the connection. Defining policy and issuing tokens are control-plane functions of the policy engine and policy administrator, and threat intelligence is an input to the engine, not a function of the enforcement point.

videos.title: Physical Security
videos.summary: Messer covers the physical controls that keep people away from equipment: bollards and barricades, access control vestibules, fencing, video surveillance, guards and access badges, lighting, and the different sensor types.
videos.deepDive:
Every technical control in this course assumes the attacker does not have physical access to the hardware. Once someone can touch a server, plug in a USB device, or walk out with a laptop, most software controls can be bypassed. Physical security is therefore the foundation layer, and the exam tests it through scenario questions that ask which physical control fits a described need. The controls fall into roughly three groups: barriers that keep people out, mechanisms that verify who may pass, and sensors that detect and record.

Barriers. Bollards and barricades are short posts or blocks that stop vehicles while letting pedestrians through. They protect building entrances and generator yards against ramming and accidental collisions, and they are visible, which adds deterrence. Fencing defines the perimeter; height, anti-climb tops, and opacity are chosen according to threat. A transparent fence lets guards see out, an opaque fence prevents reconnaissance. Fencing is both preventive and deterrent.

Controlled entry. An access control vestibule (still called a mantrap in older material) is two interlocking doors where only one can be open at a time. It stops tailgating, because a person must be individually authenticated in the space between the doors, and it can enforce one person at a time. Banks use them at data-centre and cash-vault entrances. Access badges carry a photo and usually an RFID or smart-card chip that is checked by a reader, tying entry to identity and creating an electronic log (accounting again). Security guards add human judgement: they check badges against faces, challenge unfamiliar visitors, escort contractors, and respond when a sensor fires. A guard is an operational control; a badge reader is physical and technical.

Observation and lighting. Video surveillance (CCTV) records what happens, provides evidence, and deters; modern systems add motion detection and object recognition so the SOC can be alerted rather than watching screens. Lighting is often overlooked but is a strong control: attackers avoid well-lit areas, cameras produce useful footage only with adequate light, and guards can see. Placement matters more than brightness, because glare can blind cameras and create shadows.

Sensors. The exam names four. Infrared sensors detect body heat moving through a space and are the common choice for indoor motion detection. Pressure sensors sit in floors or mats and trigger when weight is applied, useful under windows or in front of safes. Microwave sensors emit microwave energy and detect changes in the reflected signal, covering large areas and penetrating some walls, which makes them good for warehouses but prone to false alarms. Ultrasonic sensors send sound waves above human hearing and detect motion through changes in the reflection, suited to enclosed rooms. Sensors are detective controls that feed alarms and cameras.

Worked example. A fintech leasing a floor in an Ikeja office park needs to protect a small server room. A reasonable layered design: badge reader with PIN on the door (preventive, logs entry), a small vestibule if space allows (stops tailgating), infrared sensor and camera inside (detective), a sign stating the area is monitored (deterrent), and a guard at reception verifying visitors. Layering is the point: no single physical control is sufficient, and the exam often asks which control addresses a specific weakness such as tailgating (vestibule) or vehicle ramming (bollards).

keyTerms.def: A short sturdy post used to stop vehicles from reaching a protected area while allowing pedestrian access.
A small space with two interlocking doors that permits only one authenticated person to pass at a time, preventing tailgating.
A perimeter barrier that defines the boundary of a facility and deters or prevents unauthorised entry.
Camera systems that record and monitor activity, providing detection, deterrence, and evidence.
An identification card, often with RFID or smart-card technology, used to authenticate and log physical entry.
A sensor that detects heat signatures of moving bodies, commonly used for indoor motion detection.
A sensor that triggers when weight is applied to a surface such as a floor mat.
A sensor that detects motion through changes in reflected microwave signals, suited to large areas.
A sensor that detects motion by measuring changes in reflected high-frequency sound waves.

examTips: Tailgating or piggybacking through a door is solved by an access control vestibule.
Vehicle-based threats point to bollards or barricades, not fencing.
Sensor questions test the medium: heat (infrared), weight (pressure), radio (microwave), sound (ultrasonic).
Guards are operational controls; badge readers and sensors are physical or technical; signs are deterrent.
Lighting supports both cameras and guards, so it often appears as the answer to 'improve effectiveness of existing surveillance'.
videos.realWorld: In a bank, physical security data increasingly lands in the SOC: badge-reader logs, door-forced alarms, and camera analytics are integrated with the SIEM so an analyst can correlate a 2 a.m. server-room badge swipe with a suspicious login from that room. GRC analysts audit physical access lists for data centres and branch vaults, check that visitor logs and escort rules are followed, and verify that CCTV retention meets CBN and internal policy.

quiz.q: Security staff report that employees regularly hold the data-centre door open for colleagues who have not badged in. Which physical control BEST addresses this problem?
quiz.explain: An access control vestibule with interlocking doors forces each person to authenticate individually and prevents tailgating. Fencing and bollards address the perimeter and vehicles, and lighting improves visibility but does not stop someone being let in.

quiz.q: A bank wants to protect the glass front of a branch from vehicles being driven through it. Which control should be installed?
quiz.explain: Bollards are designed to stop vehicles while still allowing pedestrians to pass. Sensors and cameras detect and record but do not physically stop a vehicle, and a badge system controls pedestrian entry through doors.

quiz.q: A warehouse needs motion detection across a large open floor where the sensor signal must pass through some internal partitions. Which sensor type is MOST appropriate?
quiz.explain: Microwave sensors cover large areas and can penetrate some non-metallic barriers. Pressure sensors only detect weight on a specific surface, infrared sensors need line of sight to a heat source, and ultrasonic sensors are best suited to enclosed rooms.

videos.title: Deception and Disruption
videos.summary: Messer explains how defenders deliberately deceive attackers with honeypots, honeynets, honeyfiles, and honeytokens so that attacks are detected early and attacker techniques can be studied.
videos.deepDive:
Most security controls try to keep attackers out. Deception controls take the opposite approach: they invite attackers into a fake environment and watch what they do. The value is twofold. First, detection: a legitimate user has no reason to touch a decoy, so any interaction is a high-confidence alert with almost no false positives. Second, intelligence: by observing the attacker's tools, commands, and targets, the defenders learn what to look for on the real network and how to harden it. Deception is a detective control by nature and can also be a deterrent if attackers learn that the organisation uses it.

Honeypot. A honeypot is a single system deliberately built to look attractive to an attacker: an apparently unpatched web server, an open database, a file share named 'finance-backups'. It is isolated from production, instrumented heavily, and monitored constantly. It does not hold any real data. Because nobody legitimate should ever connect to it, every login attempt, port scan, or exploit is worth investigating. Honeypots range from low-interaction (they emulate a few services and record connection attempts) to high-interaction (a full operating system the attacker can actually compromise, giving richer intelligence but requiring careful containment so it cannot be used as a pivot).

Honeynet. A honeynet is a network of honeypots, sometimes with fake routers, workstations, and servers, built to look like a whole department or company. It lets defenders observe how an attacker moves laterally, escalates privilege, and hunts for data once inside. Many honeynets are shared research projects, and the observations feed threat-intelligence feeds that SOCs consume.

Honeyfile. A honeyfile is a decoy document placed where an attacker rummaging through a system would find it: a file called passwords.xlsx on a share, or 'board-minutes-confidential.docx' in a directory. Opening, copying, or exfiltrating the file triggers an alert. Honeyfiles are cheap, and unlike a honeypot they can live on real production systems because they are inert data. They are especially effective against insider threats and ransomware operators who search for valuable files.

Honeytoken. A honeytoken is a piece of fake data that is traceable rather than a whole file: a fake customer record in the CRM, a fake API key in a code repository, a fake email address in a mailing list, a dummy credential in a configuration file. If that record turns up in a breach dump, if that API key is ever used, or if that address receives spam, the organisation knows the data set was stolen and often from which copy. Honeytokens turn the problem of finding a needle in a haystack into waiting for the needle to announce itself.

Disruption. Beyond detection, deception can waste an attacker's time and resources: fake DNS entries that point scanners to dead ends, tarpits that hold connections open, and decoy credentials that lead to the honeynet. The goal is to make the attacker slower and noisier so the real defences have more time to respond.

Cautions. A honeypot must never be reachable from real systems in a way that lets an attacker pivot; it must be legally reviewed (entrapment is not usually an issue for defensive honeypots, but data-protection rules apply if attacker data is collected); and alerts must actually be monitored, or the deception is worthless. On the exam, match the noun: system means honeypot, network means honeynet, document means honeyfile, data element means honeytoken.

keyTerms.def: A deliberately attractive, isolated decoy system used to detect and study attackers.
A network of honeypots and decoy infrastructure designed to look like a real environment and reveal attacker behaviour.
A decoy file with an enticing name placed to trigger an alert when accessed, copied, or exfiltrated.
A fake, traceable data element such as a dummy credential, record, or API key whose use reveals that data was stolen.
A honeypot that emulates only a few services to log connection attempts with minimal risk.
A fully functional decoy system that attackers can compromise, yielding richer intelligence at higher containment cost.
A category of detective controls that use decoys to identify intrusions and gather intelligence with very few false positives.

examTips: Match the object: single system = honeypot, network = honeynet, file = honeyfile, data record or credential = honeytoken.
Any access to a decoy is a real alert because legitimate users never touch it; questions often highlight low false positives.
Honeytokens are the answer when the goal is to learn WHERE a leak came from or whether a database was stolen.
Honeypots must be isolated from production so they cannot become a pivot point.
videos.realWorld: Fintech SOCs increasingly plant honeytokens: a fake AWS access key in the repository, a fake customer with a unique email address in the production database, and a 'vpn-credentials.txt' honeyfile on file shares. When the fake key is used or the fake email gets a phishing message, the analyst knows precisely which data set was compromised. GRC teams document these as detective controls in the risk register and ensure the legal team has approved what attacker data is collected under the NDPA.

quiz.q: A security team wants to know if attackers are exploring its internal network after a phishing incident, and wants to observe how they move between systems. Which control is MOST appropriate?
quiz.explain: A honeynet is a network of decoy systems designed to reveal lateral movement and attacker techniques. A honeyfile detects access to one document, a honeytoken detects use of one data item, and a firewall blocks rather than observes.

quiz.q: A bank inserts a fabricated customer record with a unique email address into its customer database. Weeks later that address begins receiving spam. What does this indicate and what control was used?
options: The network was scanned; a honeynet
The email server is misconfigured; a honeypot
The customer database was exfiltrated; a honeytoken
A user opened a decoy document; a honeyfile
quiz.explain: A traceable fake data element that reveals a leak when it is used is a honeytoken. The unique address appearing in spam shows the database copy containing it was stolen. Honeypots and honeynets are decoy systems, and a honeyfile is a decoy document.

quiz.q: An administrator places a file named passwords.xlsx on a shared drive and configures an alert to fire whenever it is opened. Which type of control is this?
quiz.explain: A decoy document that alerts on access is a honeyfile, and because it identifies an event rather than stopping or fixing it, it is a detective control. It is not a full decoy system (honeypot), not a network of decoys (honeynet), and not a single traceable data element (honeytoken).

objectives.title: Explain the importance of change management processes and the impact to security

videos.title: Change Management
videos.summary: Messer explains why organisations formalise change: the approval process, ownership, stakeholders, impact analysis, test results, backout plans, maintenance windows, and standard operating procedures.
videos.deepDive:
Change management is the process an organisation uses to make sure that modifications to systems are planned, evaluated, approved, tested, communicated, and reversible. It exists because uncontrolled change is one of the biggest causes of outages and security incidents: a firewall rule added in a hurry that exposes a database, a patch that breaks the payment switch at month-end, a configuration tweak nobody documented so the next engineer undoes it. The exam treats change management as a security control in its own right, because every change is a chance to weaken a control, and a formal process is how those chances are caught.

The approval process. A change begins with a request that states what will change, why, when, who is responsible, what could go wrong, and how it will be undone. The request is reviewed by a change advisory board (CAB) or an equivalent group representing IT, security, and the business. The board looks for conflicts with other changes, security implications, and timing problems, then approves, rejects, or asks for more information. Emergency changes follow a shortened path but are still recorded and reviewed afterward.

Ownership and stakeholders. Every change has an owner: the person or team who requested it and who is accountable for its outcome. The owner is not necessarily the engineer doing the work; a finance manager might own a change to the reporting system that IT implements. Stakeholders are everyone affected: the business units that use the system, the support desk that will take calls, the SOC that will see new log patterns, and sometimes customers. Identifying stakeholders early is how you avoid taking a system down during their busiest hour.

Impact analysis. Before approval, someone must ask what happens if the change works and what happens if it fails. Which systems depend on this one? Could a database schema change break the mobile app? Could a security patch reboot a server that hosts a critical service? Impact analysis rates the risk and drives the amount of testing and the size of the maintenance window. A high-impact change to core banking gets a full test plan; a low-impact change to a departmental printer queue might be pre-approved as a standard change.

Test results. Changes are tried in a test or staging environment that resembles production, and the results are attached to the request. This is where you find that the patch conflicts with the antivirus agent, or that the new firewall rule blocks a backup job. No test results usually means no approval.

Backout plan. Every change needs a documented way to return to the previous state: a snapshot to restore, the previous configuration file, the old package version. The plan is written before the change, not during an outage at 3 a.m. Some changes cannot be easily reversed (a database migration that deletes columns), and the impact analysis must flag those so extra care is taken.

Maintenance window. This is the agreed time when the change may be made, chosen to minimise impact: overnight, weekends, or outside fiscal deadlines. For a Nigerian bank this means avoiding salary days, end-of-month processing, and public holidays when transaction volume spikes. The window also tells the SOC and the help desk when to expect disruption so they do not raise false incidents.

Standard operating procedures. The whole flow is written down as an SOP so it is repeated consistently regardless of who is on duty. SOPs also define what counts as a standard (pre-approved) change, a normal change, and an emergency change. In GRC terms, the SOP and the change records are the evidence auditors ask for to prove that production changes were controlled.

keyTerms.def: A formal process for requesting, evaluating, approving, testing, implementing, and documenting changes to systems to reduce risk.
The review and sign-off of a change request by authorised parties such as a change advisory board before implementation.
The individual accountable for a change's justification, outcome, and communication.
Any person or group affected by a change who should be consulted or informed about it.
The assessment of what systems, services, and users a change could affect and what the consequences of success or failure would be.
Documented evidence from a non-production environment showing that a change works as intended before it reaches production.
A pre-written procedure for restoring the previous state if a change fails.
A scheduled period during which changes may be implemented to minimise business disruption.
A documented, repeatable procedure that defines how a process such as change management is carried out.

examTips: If a scenario describes an outage after an undocumented tweak, the missing control is change management.
The backout plan is written before the change; questions about restoring the previous state point to it.
Impact analysis determines the level of testing and the size of the maintenance window.
The change owner is accountable even if a different team performs the technical work.
Emergency changes still go through approval, just after the fact and expedited.
videos.realWorld: Change management is one of the most audited processes in a bank. GRC analysts sample change tickets and check for approval, test evidence, backout plans, and post-implementation review, because regulators and ISO 27001 auditors treat missing records as a finding. SOC analysts consume the change calendar: an alert for a configuration change on a firewall is benign if it matches an approved ticket in the maintenance window and highly suspicious if it does not, so 'was this an approved change?' is often the first triage question.

quiz.q: An engineer applies a firewall rule change during business hours without a ticket, and the change blocks the bank's card-authorisation traffic for an hour. Which process would MOST likely have prevented this?
quiz.explain: A formal change management process would have required a request, impact analysis, testing, approval, and a maintenance window, any of which would have caught the risk to card traffic. Vulnerability management finds flaws, incident response handles events after they occur, and gap analysis compares posture against a standard.

quiz.q: During change planning for a database upgrade, the team documents the snapshot they will restore and the steps to reinstall the previous version if the upgrade fails. What is this document called?
quiz.explain: A backout plan is the pre-written procedure to return to the previous known-good state. Impact analysis assesses the consequences of the change, a maintenance window is the scheduled time, and an SOP is the general procedure for how changes are handled.

quiz.q: A change to the online banking platform is proposed. The security team asks which downstream systems, business units, and customer functions could be affected if the change fails. Which change-management activity is being performed?
quiz.explain: Identifying the systems and people that a change could affect and the consequences of failure is impact analysis. Approval is the sign-off that follows, backout planning defines how to reverse the change, and version control tracks configuration or code revisions.

videos.title: Technical Change Management
videos.summary: Messer describes the technical side of implementing a change: allow and deny lists, restricted activities, downtime, service and application restarts, dependencies, documentation, and version control.
videos.deepDive:
The previous video covered the administrative process of approving a change. This one covers what actually happens when the engineer touches the system, and the technical decisions that determine whether a change is safe. The exam tests this by giving you a change scenario and asking which technical consideration was missed. The recurring lesson is that a change almost never affects only the component you intended to modify.

Allow lists and deny lists. Many organisations control which applications may run using an allow list (only listed software runs; everything else is blocked) or a deny list (listed software is blocked; everything else runs). Allow lists are far more secure but require that every legitimate update be added before deployment, so a change that installs a new version of an application must include updating the allow list or the software will be blocked on rollout. Deny lists are easier to manage but only stop known-bad software. Change tickets should state which list needs modification.

Restricted activities. The change approval covers a specific scope. If the ticket says 'upgrade the database engine', the engineer may not also patch the operating system, change firewall rules, or clean up user accounts while they are logged in, however tempting. Scope creep inside a maintenance window is a classic cause of unexplained outages and it defeats the testing that was done for the approved scope. If additional work is needed, it gets its own change.

Downtime. Some changes require a service to be unavailable. The ticket must state the expected downtime, and the team should look for ways to reduce it: performing the change on a secondary node and failing over, using rolling upgrades in a cluster, or doing the work in the maintenance window when volume is lowest. Users and the help desk must be informed in advance so they do not report an incident. In 24-hour environments such as payment switches, near-zero downtime designs are the norm and the change plan must describe them.

Service and application restarts. Many changes only take effect after a service, an application, or the whole operating system restarts. A kernel patch on a Linux server needs a reboot; a configuration change to a web server may need only a service reload. The plan must state what will be restarted, how long it takes, and what monitoring will confirm it came back healthy. A reboot that hangs at 2 a.m. with no one watching is a self-inflicted availability incident.

Dependencies. Modern systems are chains. Upgrading a library may require upgrading the application that uses it; upgrading the application may require a newer database driver; the database driver may need a newer operating system. Changes must map these dependencies in advance and sequence them correctly. A dependency that was missed shows up as an application that will not start after an otherwise successful change.

Documentation. After the change, network diagrams, configuration records, runbooks, and asset inventories must be updated. Documentation drift is a security problem: the SOC investigates against the diagram they have, and if it is wrong, they draw wrong conclusions. Good change tickets include a documentation task as a required step.

Version control. Configuration files, scripts, firewall rule sets, and infrastructure-as-code templates should live in a version control system such as Git. Every change is a commit with an author, a timestamp, and a diff, which gives accountability, makes review possible, and makes the backout plan as simple as reverting to the previous version. Version control also detects unauthorised change: if the running configuration differs from the committed one, something happened outside the process.

Worked example. A fintech upgrades its payment API. The plan updates the application allow list on the servers, notes that the new API needs a newer TLS library (dependency), schedules a 20-minute rolling restart across three nodes so the service never fully drops (downtime and restart), forbids any other work on the servers during the window (restricted activity), commits the new configuration to Git (version control), and assigns the architect to update the diagram (documentation).

keyTerms.def: A list of explicitly permitted applications or entities; anything not on the list is blocked.
A list of explicitly blocked applications or entities; anything not on the list is permitted.
The rule that work performed during a change is limited to the approved scope.
The period during which a service is unavailable because of a change; it must be planned, minimised, and communicated.
Stopping and starting a service or application so that a change takes effect, which must be planned and monitored.
A component that another component requires; changes must account for the chain of dependencies.
The updated diagrams, configurations, and procedures that must be revised after a change to keep records accurate.
A system that tracks every revision of code or configuration with author, time, and differences, enabling review and rollback.

examTips: Allow lists block everything not listed, so a software update can fail until the list is updated; deny lists only stop known-bad software.
If a change to one component breaks another, the missed step is dependency analysis.
Doing extra unapproved work during a change window violates restricted activities.
Version control is the answer for tracking who changed a configuration and rolling it back.
Outdated diagrams after a change point to a documentation failure.
videos.realWorld: In practice a SOC analyst sees the effects of technical change management every shift: a burst of failed application launches after an allow-list update was forgotten, a server that never came back after a planned restart, or a configuration diff alert from a tool comparing running firewall rules to the Git repository. GRC analysts test that configuration baselines are in version control and that post-change documentation is current, because auditors reviewing a bank's network diagram expect it to match reality.

quiz.q: After a scheduled application upgrade, users on managed workstations report that the new version will not launch, while the old version worked. The upgrade was tested successfully on an engineer's unmanaged laptop. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The backout plan was not executed
The deny list blocked the old version
The maintenance window was too short
The application allow list was not updated for the new version
quiz.explain: Managed workstations typically enforce an application allow list; the new executable was not on it, so it was blocked. The engineer's unmanaged laptop had no such control, which is why testing passed. The maintenance window length does not affect execution, the backout plan is for reversal, and a deny list blocking the old version would not explain the new version failing.

quiz.q: While applying an approved database patch during a maintenance window, an administrator also decides to remove several old user accounts and adjust firewall rules on the same server. Which change-management principle has been violated?
quiz.explain: Work during a change must stay within the approved scope. Adding unapproved tasks is a violation of restricted activities and undermines the testing and approval that covered only the patch. Dependencies, version control, and documentation are separate considerations.

quiz.q: A security team wants to know who modified a firewall configuration file, what exactly changed, and be able to revert to the prior configuration quickly. Which practice BEST provides this?
quiz.explain: Version control records each revision with the author, timestamp, and the exact differences, and allows a previous version to be restored. Maintenance windows schedule the work, impact analysis evaluates consequences in advance, and restarts apply changes but do not track them.

objectives.title: Explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions

videos.title: Public Key Infrastructure
videos.summary: Messer introduces symmetric versus asymmetric encryption, how public and private key pairs are generated and used, and the idea of key escrow within a public key infrastructure.
videos.deepDive:
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the collection of policies, procedures, software, and hardware that lets an organisation create, distribute, manage, store, and revoke digital certificates and the key pairs behind them. To understand why PKI is needed, you first have to understand the two families of encryption and the problem each one leaves unsolved.

Symmetric encryption. One key encrypts and the same key decrypts. AES is the standard example. Symmetric algorithms are fast and produce compact output, so they are used for bulk data: disks, databases, the actual bytes of a TLS session. The weakness is key distribution. If Ada in Lagos wants to send Bayo in Abuja an AES-encrypted file, Bayo needs the same key, and sending the key over the same untrusted network defeats the purpose. With many parties the problem explodes: each pair needs its own secret, so a thousand users need roughly half a million keys.

Asymmetric encryption. Each party generates a mathematically linked pair: a public key that can be given to anyone and a private key that is never shared. Something encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key, and something signed with the private key can be verified with the public key. RSA and elliptic-curve algorithms are the common examples. Now Ada simply fetches Bayo's public key, encrypts the file, and only Bayo's private key can open it. No secret ever travels. The cost is speed: asymmetric operations are far slower and are unsuitable for large data.

Key generation. The key pair is created together in one operation from a large random number and the algorithm's mathematics (for RSA, two large primes). The security of the scheme depends on the fact that deriving the private key from the public key is computationally infeasible at the chosen key length. The private key must be generated and stored securely, ideally in hardware, because anyone who obtains it can decrypt everything encrypted to the public key and sign as the owner.

How the two families are used together. In practice almost every real system is hybrid. Asymmetric cryptography is used to authenticate parties and to securely deliver a symmetric session key; the symmetric key then protects the bulk data. TLS, S/MIME, and VPNs all work this way. A common exam question describes a process and asks which key is used at which step: encrypt to the recipient's public key, decrypt with the recipient's private key, sign with the sender's private key, verify with the sender's public key.

Why PKI exists. Asymmetric encryption solves distribution but creates a new problem: how does Ada know that the public key she fetched really belongs to Bayo and not to an attacker in the middle? PKI answers this with certificates: a trusted certificate authority verifies Bayo's identity and signs a document binding his name to his public key. Ada trusts the CA, so she trusts the binding. PKI also handles the full lifecycle: issuing, renewing, revoking, and archiving keys, and defining who may do each.

Key escrow. Key escrow means a trusted third party (often the organisation itself, sometimes a government or a regulator) holds a copy of private keys or decryption keys.
